Instead, focus on your own circumstances, capacity, or a neutral change in direction. Here are a few scripts, from softer to more direct (but still kind):

### 1. The “bandwidth” approach (white lie, but kind)
> “I’ve got a lot on my plate at the moment and just can’t give the applications the time they deserve. I hope you understand.”

This doesn’t blame anyone and is hard to argue with. If they push, you can repeat, “I wish I could, but I’m stretched too thin right now.”

### 2. The skills-based redirect
> “I think I’ve taken this as far as I can. I’m not really an expert, and I’d hate to give you bad advice. Maybe [local job centre, charity, online resource] would be more helpful?”

This frames it as you hitting your limits, not a comment on their follow-through.

### 3. The gentle boundary with an exit ramp
> “I’ve enjoyed helping, but I’ve realised I need to focus on some personal stuff. I’m going to step back from the application sessions. If you ever need a second pair of eyes quickly on something, feel free to ask, but I can’t do the regular sessions anymore.”

This leaves a tiny door open if they ever do get serious, without committing you.

### 4. If you want to be a touch more honest (but still respectful)
> “I’ve noticed the applications we’ve worked on haven’t been sent off, and I’m not sure my help is actually meeting your needs right now. Maybe we should pause until you’re feeling more ready to take that step—no pressure.”

This turns it into a conversation about their readiness, not a judgment on their entire community. It gives them a chance to explain, and you might be surprised.

If your real reason is the hopelessness you feel about the situation (“nobody down there was ever going to use them”), you might want to sit with that privately. Is it possible you’re burnt out or disillusioned? That’s valid, but it’s a separate issue from what you say to your neighbour. Telling someone outright “I stopped because people like you never follow through” would be cruel even if it felt true in the moment.

For what to say, I’d lean toward option 1 or 2—simple, clean, and impossible to reframe as an attack. If the neighbour asks why you’ve “really” stopped, you can just say, “Life’s got busy, honestly,” and change the subject.

Take care with your own boundaries, but also try to leave the door ajar for kindness. Sometimes the help we give isn’t wasted, even when the paperwork gathers dust—it reminds people they’re worth investing in.
